newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: US envoy backs Mladic's dismissal.
newsitem.headline: US envoy backs Mladic's dismissal.

text.p: A U.S. envoy for Bosnia on Tuesday backed the Bosnian Serb authorities in their standoff with sacked Serb army commander General Ratko Mladic, who raised the stakes by warning of possible fratricidal war.
"The fact that General Mladic has been relieved (of his command) was a step forward," Ambassador John Kornblum told reporters in Belgrade after meeting Serbia's President Slobodan Milosevic.
"We expect Yugoslavia and (Milosevic)... to support the decision of the government of the Bosnian Serb republic."

Bosnian Serb president Biljana Plavsic dismissed Mladic and the general staff last weekend but he and his loyal wartime officers are resisting the dismissal, raising tensions in the Bosnian Serb republic.
Mladic's sacking was regarded as an attempt by the government to regain civilian political control over the Bosnian Serb army (BSA).
Along with former Serb president Radovan Karadzic, he has been indicted twice for war crimes by an international tribunal in The Hague.
Mladic, reported to be ailing, kept a low profile and helped implement the military aspects of the Dayton peace accord, but retained the army's loyalty.
A hero among the Serbs, Mladic survived a similar attempt to sack him last year, but the army has been weakened since peace was restored and the civilian police have grown in influence.
On Tuesday evening the ousted Bosnian Serb army general staff issued a veiled threat to their main rivals, the police loyal to civilian authorities.
"We plead to them not to allow services, bodies and units of the (Bosnian Serb) police to be pushed into a fratricidal war," it said in a statement faxed to Reuters.

It warned the Bosnian Serb Ministry of the Interior not to place its forces "into the columns of enemies who, in various ways, are opening the doors of the Balkans for the permanent deployment of foreign military troops".
The statement accused the police of cooperating with the NATO-led peacekeeping force IFOR "in order to plan joint actions against...the BSA".
It warned the ministry that similar police action led to the downfall of the Serb Krajina enclave in Croatia in 1995.

It quoted a NATO official as saying that anything that diminished the Bosnian Serb army's power and unity was in the interests of NATO and that "such a situation leads towards reintegration of Bosnia and Herzegovina".
The language used in the statement, stoking resentment towards NATO, and the veiled threats were bound to infuriate Milosevic, military analysts said.
They doubted Mladic could last long in the "palace coup" against him, especially after apparently losing the Serbian leader's support.

Diplomats suspected Milosevic was behind the purge of Bosnian Serb generals for domestic and foreign policy reasons, as he strives to wipe the slate clean of war-time accomplices in his new pursuit of peace in the Balkans and acceptance overseas.

Milosevic, the guarantor of Bosnian Serb compliance with the Dayton peace agreement, needs to convince the West of his commitment to peace in order to get the remaining sanctions against Yugoslavia lifted.
Analysts describe Mladic as a wild card and liability now that the peace process has entered its second year.
Hours before his dismissal, the Belgrade newspaper Politika, close to Milosevic, issued a rare rebuke to the Bosnian Serb army for interfering in civilian affairs.
Kornblum said he had asked Milosevic to ensure that Mladic would step down.
Milosevic "just said that he assumed the decision by the (Serb) government would stand. I accept that," Kornblum said.
